content.text:
Plan a story of about 500 words from this premise.

Write a touching short story about a young person from a small town. Approximately 500 words.

Propose about 1 scenes of roughly 500 words each. Give every character, location and significant object a stable id now — later scenes can only refer to entities that exist. State the world rules the story must not break. Then call submit_plan.

entities.sketch: Ellie, 19, a small-town girl with paint-smudged fingers and a stubborn, gentle steadiness. Leaving Marlow for art school but tied to the town by memory and a promise.
Mr. Hart, late 60s, retired mechanic and neighbor; knits without fuss, carves wood in his shed, and has been a quiet guardian figure in Ellie's life.
Rufus, a limping stray dog Ellie adopted, patchy fur and an old collar; follows her everywhere and understands small rituals.
The single-track rail platform at the edge of Marlow: low brick wall, a battered bench, and the view down the main street toward the sea. The town's small departures happen here.
Marlow's main street: a line of low shops, the bakery with its bell, the postbox, and the narrow lane leading toward Mr. Hart's house and the platform.

Ellie's sketchbook: a soft-covered, cloth-bound notebook with corners bent and the spine taped where pages once threatened to fall out. Inside are drawings of small-town details and notes she never shares often.
A small, hand-carved wooden boat, varnished smooth, the work of Mr. Hart. He gave it to Ellie when she was a child; she has carried it as a talisman for years.
A worn, grey suitcase patched with duct tape and a strip of blue cloth from Ellie's mother. It carries the practical and sentimental fragments she's willing to take.

arguments.logline: On the single platform of her hometown, a young artist about to leave for art school says a quiet goodbye to the place and people who raised her; a carved wooden boat and a dog stand between the life she leaves and the one she will make, and a small, ordinary blessing from an old neighbor gives her the courage to go.

scenes.intent: A single, roughly 500-word scene showing Ellie on Marlow's platform the morning she leaves. The scene should: 1) Make the reader feel the weight and sweetness of a small-town farewell through sensory details — the smell of baking, the hiss of a kettle through an open window, the grain of the wooden boat in Ellie's palms. 2) Use objects (obj-notebook, obj-carved-boat, obj-suitcase) as emotional anchors that reveal Ellie's history without lengthy exposition. 3) Show Mr. Hart's quiet blessing — a short, specific action (a carved wooden sail added to the boat, a folded note tucked into the notebook, or an extra seam of varnish) rather than a speech — that makes the goodbye possible. 4) Let Rufus the dog act as a tether between Ellie's past and future. 5) End on a modest, open note: the train arrives, Ellie steps aboard holding the boat and notebook; she does not close the door on the town but keeps a small, ordinary object that will carry the reader's sense of continuity. Tone should be tender, unflashy, and precise; show rather than tell. Target length: approximately 500 words.

world_rules: No supernatural events or magical realism: everything must be explicable in ordinary terms.
Character ages and identities are fixed by their entity sketches and must not be contradicted later (e.g., char-ellie is 19; char-mr-hart is late 60s).
Objects retain continuity: an object given in one scene (e.g., obj-carved-boat) exists in future scenes and may carry wear or notes explaining its condition.
Geography is consistent: Marlow is a small town with a single rail platform and a main street as described — distances and directions should not be contradicted.
No retroactive retcons without an explicit index entry: any change to these facts must be recorded in the project's continuity files with provenance.

Half of the score on this kind of task is length compliance, so if the committed scenes are running short of their targets, say so in the writer's brief — it cannot see this number and will otherwise keep writing to the same length.
The sequence is fixed and enforced: call_context_builder, then call_writer, then
call_verifier, then call_index_manager once it is approved. A call out of order comes
back as a refusal naming the legal next step. Repairs loop between call_writer and
call_verifier.
Allowance for this scene (middle, position 0.5 of the story): 3 repair round(s), 3 follow-up question(s) for the writer, 2 previous scene(s) of prose in the packet.
Why: middle third: enough is on the page now that this scene has to agree with it, and the material a contradiction would live in is no longer all in front of you. Ask before drafting rather than repairing afterwards; a question costs a fraction of a repair round.
It is a ceiling, not a quota. Spending a repair round on a defect the writer cannot see how to fix buys the same draft again — a finding that survives a rewrite unchanged ends the loop whatever the allowance says.

Open promises: none recorded.

Nothing is planned after this one: this is the last scene.
That block is assembled for you so that judging the plan does not depend on your
going to look for it. You still have `bash` and `read` over the whole project — the
committed scenes under novel/chapters/, the outline, the promise ledger, the rhythm
file — and the block is a starting point rather than the limit. If the prose has
outgrown the plan for the scenes ahead, `update_plan` now: you cannot touch scenes
already written, and after this one is committed it joins them.
Each call takes a `brief`: what is particular about this scene. The specialists keep
their own sessions and already know their jobs, so a brief that restates their role
wastes a turn. Say what this scene needs that the last one did not.

**This is the last scene, so it has to end the story.** Not gesture at an ending —
end it. If the premise poses a question, this scene answers it: who, how, and how the
impossibility was possible. A detective story that closes on "there is enough for a
warrant" has not finished; it has stopped.

Two specific ways this has gone wrong here. The writer wrote a confrontation in which
nobody was named and every contradiction the story had carefully listed was left
standing — and then declared the promise paid off, so the ledger, the revision pass
and the finding count all agreed the book was complete. Say in the brief that the
answer must be *on the page*, in the prose, not implied by the arrangement of clues.

And check it yourself before you commit. You can read the draft; read the last few
paragraphs and ask whether a reader who stopped there would know what happened. If
they would not, send it back — this is what your repair rounds are for, and it is the
one defect no later scene can fix.
Finish when the scene is committed or you have abandoned it. Then say in two or three
sentences what happened: how many attempts, what the verifier objected to, where the
artefacts are.

Ensure no contradictions with submitted plan and world rules.

- Ellie, nineteen, waits on Marlow’s single platform before dawn, smells of the bakery and the hiss of a kettle from nearby houses framing the morning.
